strategy_title: Increasing Block Size via Autotune Causes Regression
strategy_description: Increasing XBLOCK from 128 to 512 via @triton.autotune improved compute SM throughput (25% → 71%) and occupancy (36.8% → 66.7%), but caused a 1.72x slowdown in wall-clock duration (31.23 µs → 53.86 µs). The critical flaw is that the grid was NOT updated to use a lambda — the grid remained hardcoded as `triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128)`, so the grid size stayed at 47,040 CTAs while each CTA now processed 512 elements, causing 4x more total work (executed instructions jumped from 6.2M to 30.2M). When adding autotune to a pointwise kernel, the grid computation must also be made dynamic (lambda meta: triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK'])) to match the selected tile size.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: fixed grid, fixed XBLOCK
grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)
kernel[grid](arg_0, arg_1, xnumel, XBLOCK=128)
applicable_when: Pointwise kernels with low achieved occupancy (<50%), high L1TEX stall cycles (>70% of warp cycles), low eligible warps per scheduler (<0.5), and small block sizes (≤128) relative to available register headroom.
do_not_apply_when: When the grid is not updated to be a dynamic lambda matching the autotune XBLOCK — this causes the kernel to process each element multiple times, multiplying instruction count and causing severe regression. Also avoid when register count per thread is high (>32) and larger blocks would hit register limits.
framework_notes: In Triton, when using @triton.autotune, the grid MUST be a lambda: `lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(N, meta['XBLOCK']),)`. A static grid computed with the old XBLOCK will not shrink when autotune selects a larger block, causing redundant work. The explicit XBLOCK argument must also be removed from the kernel call — autotune injects it automatically.
